questions.question: Are we on pace to hit goal, and where do we land by election day if nothing changes?

args.query: projection method on pace goal election day

sources.text: Pace compares doors to date with the goal to date. The projection for Election Day assumes nothing changes: doors to date plus the average daily doors of the last 7 days times the knocking days left. An office "will miss goal" when its projection is below its total goal; the shortfall is the goal minus the projection.

questions.answer:
We're ahead of goal to date (103.3% of the goal-to-date), but if nothing changes we land short of the full goal by about 3,300 doors — roughly 94.6% of the 60,632 total.

- Program doors to date: 33,503 vs goal-to-date 32,431 = 103.3% [table:v_office_pace]
- Projected total by election day: 57,329, which is -3,303 vs the 60,632 goal (94.6%) [table:v_office_pace]
- Northside is the only office over goal: projected 23,583 = 104% (+908) [table:v_office_pace]
- Harbor: projected 19,150 = 95% (-1,007) [table:v_office_pace]
- Eastgate is the biggest gap: projected 14,596 = 82% (-3,204) [table:v_office_pace]
- To close the gap we'd need about 4.1 extra shifts per day program-wide (Eastgate 4.4, Harbor 1.3, Northside 0) [table:v_office_pace]

How it's worked out: the projection assumes nothing changes — doors to date plus the last 7 days' average daily doors (1,489.1) × 16 knocking days left (Oct 19 to Nov 3); an office "will miss goal" when its projection is below its total goal [doc:program-plan#pace-and-projection].

questions.question: Based on our pace and what's left, should we ask the client for more doors, or a second pass on the turf we have?

args.query: more doors or a second pass decision

args.sql: SELECT office, SUM(doors_untouched) AS untouched, SUM(not_home_doors) AS not_home FROM v_precinct_coverage GROUP BY office ORDER BY office

sources.text: When projected capacity for the rest of the program (average daily doors of the last 7 days times days left) is larger than the untouched doors left in our turf, we will run out of first-pass turf. In that case ask the client for more doors first; new turf contacts voters at the normal first-pass rate. A second pass on not-home doors is the fallback, because second passes contact voters at roughly half the first-pass rate. If untouched doors exceed capacity, keep working the turf we have.

questions.answer:
Ask the client for more doors — the program will run out of first-pass turf before Election Day, so new turf is the right ask, with a second pass on not-home doors only as the fallback.

- Program capacity left: 1,489.1 doors/day × 16 days = 23,826 doors [table:v_office_pace]
- First-pass turf left (untouched doors): 10,393 across all offices (Eastgate 1,183, Harbor 8,096, Northside 1,114) [table:v_precinct_coverage]
- Capacity exceeds untouched turf by about 13,433 doors, so we will run out of first-pass turf [table:v_office_pace]
- Not-home doors available for a second pass: 18,555 (Eastgate 4,712, Harbor 6,418, Northside 7,425) [table:v_precinct_coverage]
- The shortfall is concentrated in Eastgate (projected 3,204 doors short) and Harbor (1,007 short); Northside is projected 908 over [table:v_office_pace]

How it's decided: when projected capacity (last 7 days' average daily doors × days left) is larger than the untouched doors left in our turf, we run out of first-pass turf and should ask the client for more doors first, since new turf contacts voters at the normal first-pass rate; a second pass on not-home doors is the fallback because it contacts voters at roughly half the first-pass rate. [doc:program-plan#more-doors-or-a-second-pass]

args.sql: SELECT * FROM v_office_pace WHERE goal_total IS NOT NULL AND goal_to_date IS NOT NULL AND doors_to_date IS NOT NULL AND goal_total > doors_to_date AND office IN ('Northside', 'Eastgate', 'Harbor') ORDER BY office, goal_total - doors_to_date DESC LIMIT 10;

- **Harbor**: 105.3% of the goal completed, with 16 knocking days left. The projected total is 19,150 doors, which is 1,007 doors over the goal.

Given that Harbor and Northside are ahead of their goals, they might not need additional doors. However, Eastgate is behind and could benefit from either more doors or a second pass on the turf they have.

To make a decision, we should also consider the average daily doors per shift and the number of shifts needed. Eastgate has an average of 45.9 doors per shift, which is lower than the needed 12.6 doors per shift. This suggests that a second pass on the current turf might be more effective.

questions.question: Why does the client's daily report show more doors than our dashboard for Oct 12?

args.query: why client daily report shows more doors than our dashboard

args.sql: SELECT d.office, d.doors, d.attempts, d.rolled_back_attempts, c.doors_reported, c.doors_reported - d.doors AS gap FROM v_daily_doors d JOIN client_daily_report c ON c.office = d.office AND c.report_date = d.knock_date WHERE d.knock_date = '2026-10-12' ORDER BY d.office

sources.text: The client daily report counts attempts, pulled at the end of each day before any QC rollback. Our dashboard counts doors with rollbacks removed. The gap on any day is the repeat attempts at the same door plus any attempts that were later rolled back. A normal day shows a gap of a few percent from repeat attempts. A larger gap almost always means a rollback.

questions.answer:
The client's daily report counts attempts (labeled "doors") pulled at the end of each day before any QC rollback, while our dashboard counts doors with rollbacks removed — so the gap is repeat attempts at the same door plus any attempts later rolled back.

- Eastgate: client reported 498 vs our 342 doors, a gap of 156, driven by 142 rolled-back attempts [table:v_daily_doors] [table:client_daily_report]
- Harbor: client reported 428 vs our 406 doors, a gap of 22 (no rollbacks, so all repeat attempts) [table:v_daily_doors] [table:client_daily_report]
- Northside: client reported 558 vs our 533 doors, a gap of 25 (no rollbacks, so all repeat attempts) [table:v_daily_doors] [table:client_daily_report]
- A normal day shows a gap of a few percent from repeat attempts; a larger gap almost always means a rollback [doc:counting-doors#why-the-client-s-numbers-differ-from-ours]
- Eastgate's much larger gap is the exception, consistent with a rollback that day [doc:counting-doors#why-the-client-s-numbers-differ-from-ours]

How it's worked out: the client's "doors" = attempts before rollback; our doors = attempts minus repeat attempts at the same door and minus rolled-back attempts, so gap = repeat attempts + rolled-back attempts [doc:counting-doors#why-the-client-s-numbers-differ-from-ours].

sources.text: A new office should sit closest to the doors we still need: the untouched doors in our turf, weighted by how many doors each precinct has left. Untouched or lightly touched precincts (under 25 percent of doors touched) that are dense (over 2,000 doors per square mile) are worth a new office; sparse precincts (under 1,000 doors per square mile) are slow to knock and are better handled at the end with drive-out shifts. questions.answer:
Seven precincts are untouched (0% touched) and none are in the "light" band, so the remaining work is split between dense precincts worth knocking and sparse ones that are slow to cover.

**Untouched precincts (0% touched):**

  - Precinct 39 (Harbor): 1,788 doors, 4,094 doors/sq mi [table:v_precinct_coverage]

  - Precinct 11 (Northside): 890 doors, 530 doors/sq mi [table:v_precinct_coverage]
  - Precinct 36 (Harbor): 766 doors, 398 doors/sq mi [table:v_precinct_coverage]

**Is what's left dense enough to knock efficiently?**
- Yes for the four Harbor precincts (37–40): all sit well above the 2,000 doors/sq mi density bar, so they are worth knocking now — and per the plan, dense untouched precincts are exactly what a new office should sit closest to [doc:program-plan#opening-another-office].

How the density test is applied: untouched or lightly touched precincts (under 25% of doors touched) that are dense (over 2,000 doors/sq mi) are worth a new office, while sparse precincts (under 1,000 doors/sq mi) are slow to knock and are better handled at the end with drive-out shifts [doc:program-plan#opening-another-office].

questions.question: Are we on pace for the registration goal, and what cards per hour do we need from here?

args.query: registration pace projection method cards per hour needed

sources.text: Cards per hour is valid cards divided by paid registration hours. Current pace uses the last 7 days. The cards per hour needed from here is the cards still needed (goal minus valid cards) divided by the hours we expect to work before the deadline: average daily registration hours of the last 7 days times days left. An office is under the needed rate when its last 7 days rate is below the program-wide rate needed.

questions.answer:

args.query: QC calls, confirmation, unreachable, wrong information

sources.text: A sample of valid cards gets a QC call a day or two after collection. Outcomes are confirmed (the registrant confirms they filled out the card), unreachable (no answer after two tries) and wrong_info (the person says the details are wrong or they did not register). Wrong information above 10 percent of calls for a canvasser is escalated.

When QC confirms flash knocking, the knocks in the flagged window are rolled back: they stay in the data with rolled_back = true but are removed from doors and contacts. Rollbacks happen after the day's client report has been pulled, so they never change a report that was already sent.

questions.question: Who's over the weekly overtime threshold, and whose hours still need fixing or approval before payroll runs?

args.query: overtime approval rule and payroll deadline

sources.text: Payroll for the week that ended Sunday runs Tuesday at noon. Every shift must be approved by Monday at 5 PM; pending and needs_fix shifts left after that roll to the next payroll.

The overtime threshold is 40 paid hours in a payroll week, Monday through Sunday, counting every shift the person worked. Hours over 40 are paid at 1.5 times the hourly rate. Any shift that takes a person over 40 hours needs the field director's approval and stays pending until it is approved.

A shift marked needs_fix cannot be paid until a field lead corrects it. Common reasons are a missing clock out (no paid hours yet) and a shift clocked under the wrong office. Fix the record, then mark it approved.

A needs_fix shift can't be paid until a field lead corrects it (missing clock out or wrong office) [doc:payroll-rules#shifts-that-need-fixing]. Payroll runs Tuesday at noon and every shift must be approved by Monday 5 PM, or it rolls to the next payroll [doc:payroll-rules#payroll-deadline].
